q: The SI unit in which a quantity of heat is measured is the:
x: Heat is energy in transfer, so its SI unit is the joule. The kelvin measures temperature, the watt measures power, and the calorie is an older non-SI unit.

q: Two bodies at exactly the same temperature but with different masses are placed in contact. The net flow of heat between them is:
o: From the larger body to the smaller one
From the smaller body to the larger one
From the body with more internal energy to the other
x: Net heat flow depends only on a temperature difference. With equal temperatures there is none, whatever the masses or internal energies.

q: A refrigerator moves thermal energy from its cold inside to the warmer kitchen. It needs electrical energy to do this because:
o: Heat always flows from a smaller body to a larger one
The kitchen has less internal energy than the inside
Heat does not flow on its own from a colder body to a hotter one
Cold flows out of the refrigerator into the kitchen
x: Left alone, thermal energy flows only from higher to lower temperature. Moving it the other way needs work to be done, which the compressor supplies.

q: Hot water at 80 °C is added to 1 kg of cold water at 20 °C until the mixture reaches 40 °C. Ignoring heat losses, the mass of hot water added is:
x: Heat lost = heat gained: m × c × (80 − 40) = 1 × c × (40 − 20), so 40m = 20 and m = 0.5 kg.

q: When you hold a piece of ice, your hand feels cold. This is because:
o: Thermal energy flows from your hand to the ice
Coldness flows from the ice into your hand
Thermal energy flows from the ice to your hand
No energy is transferred between them
x: Your hand is at a higher temperature than the ice, so thermal energy flows out of your hand into the ice; losing heat is what feels cold.

q: The temperature of a cup of tea falls from 80 °C to 50 °C. The fall in temperature on the kelvin scale is:
x: One kelvin and one degree Celsius are the same size step, so a temperature difference of 30 °C is also 30 K. Only actual temperatures differ by 273.

q: A 1 kg copper block (specific heat 420 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 100 °C is dropped into 0.1 kg of water (specific heat 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 20 °C. Ignoring losses, the final common temperature is:
x: The heat capacities are equal: 1 × 420 = 0.1 × 4200 = 420 J K⁻¹. So the block falls and the water rises by equal amounts, meeting halfway at 60 °C.

q: A student records the heat needed per mole per kelvin for a gas. The SI unit she should write is:
x: Molar specific heat is heat per mole per kelvin, so its unit is J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the unit of specific heat, and J K⁻¹ is that of heat capacity.

q: A metal of molar mass 50 g mol⁻¹ has a specific heat of 500 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 mol of it by 1 K is:
x: 1 mol has a mass of 0.05 kg, so heat = 0.05 × 500 × 1 = 25 J. Using 50 kg instead of 0.05 kg gives 25 000 J.

q: Two substances have the same specific heat but different molar masses. Their molar specific heats are:
o: In the same ratio as their molar masses
In the inverse ratio of their molar masses
x: Molar specific heat C = Mc. With the same c, C is proportional to the molar mass M.

q: When comparing the heat needed by different gases, molar specific heat is often more useful than specific heat because:
o: One kilogram of every gas has the same volume
Specific heat cannot be measured for a gas
One mole of every gas contains the same number of molecules
Molar specific heat does not depend on the gas at all
x: One mole of any substance has the same number of molecules (Avogadro's number), so molar specific heat compares heat needed per molecule on a fair basis.

q: In the equation Q = nCΔT, where n is the number of moles, the quantity C is the:
o: Heat capacity of the whole body
x: With amount measured in moles, the constant is the molar specific heat. In Q = mcΔT, with mass in kg, c is the specific heat.

q: A beaker holds just 1 g of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Warming it through 1 K takes:
x: 1 g = 0.001 kg, so Q = 0.001 × 4200 × 1 = 4.2 J. Forgetting to change grams into kilograms gives 4200 J.

q: Half a mole of water (18 g per mole) is warmed through 10 K. If water needs 4.2 kJ per kg per kelvin, the energy required is:
x: Mass = 0.5 × 0.018 = 0.009 kg. Q = 0.009 × 4200 × 10 = 378 J. Taking 1 mol (0.018 kg) gives 756 J; treating 0.5 mol as 0.5 kg gives 21 000 J.

q: When a gas expands and pushes back its surroundings, the work done by the gas is:
x: In an expansion the gas pushes the piston outward in the direction of its force, so the work done by the gas is positive.

q: A gas does 500 J of work while expanding at a constant pressure of 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa. The increase in its volume is:
x: W = PΔV, so ΔV = 500 ÷ (2.5 × 10⁵) = 2 × 10⁻³ m³. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 1.25 × 10⁸.

q: A gas at pressure P pushes a piston of area A outward through a small distance Δx. The result W = PΔV follows from:
o: Work = force PA × distance Δx, and AΔx is the change in volume
x: The gas exerts force F = PA on the piston. W = FΔx = PAΔx, and AΔx is the volume swept, ΔV, so W = PΔV.

q: On a pressure–volume graph, a change of a gas is shown by a vertical straight line. The work done by the gas in this change is:
o: Equal to P × V at the top of the line
Equal to the length of the line
x: A vertical line means the volume does not change (only the pressure does). With ΔV = 0 the area under the line is zero, so no work is done.

q: A gas is taken round a complete cycle that forms a closed loop on a pressure–volume graph. The net work done by the gas in one cycle equals the:
o: Area under the upper part of the loop only
Highest pressure multiplied by the lowest volume
x: The work done in expansion minus the work done on the gas in compression equals the area inside the loop on the P–V graph.

q: An ideal gas expands isothermally from volume V to 2V, starting at pressure P. Compared with P × V, the work done by the gas is:
o: Equal to P × V, because the temperature is constant
Greater than P × V, because the volume doubles
Zero, because the temperature does not change
Less than P × V, because the pressure falls during the expansion
x: P × V would be the work if the pressure stayed at P. In isothermal expansion the pressure falls from P to P/2, so the area under the curve is less than PV.

q: A gas sample occupies 2 litres at 300 K under a steady 1 × 10⁵ Pa. It is warmed to 450 K with the pressure unchanged. How much work does it do on its surroundings? (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³)
x: At constant pressure V ∝ T, so V = 2 × 450/300 = 3 litres. ΔV = 1 × 10⁻³ m³, so W = 1 × 10⁵ × 1 × 10⁻³ = 100 J. Using the final volume gives 300 J.

q: A substance with a high specific heat is one that:
o: Heats up very quickly when given a little heat
Needs a lot of heat to raise the temperature of each kilogram by 1 K
x: Specific heat is the heat needed per kilogram per kelvin. A high value means much heat is needed for a small temperature rise.

q: Warming 0.2 kg of cooking oil through 15 K takes how many joules, if the oil's specific heat is 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹?
x: Q = mcΔT = 0.2 × 2000 × 15 = 6000 J. Using 2 kg instead of 0.2 kg gives the wrong 60 000 J.

q: 4200 J of heat is given to 0.5 kg of water (specific heat 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Its temperature rises by:
3 mol of an ideal gas with Cp = 29 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is heated at constant pressure through 10 K. The heat supplied is:
x: Q = nCpΔT = 3 × 29 × 10 = 870 J. Forgetting the number of moles gives 290 J.

q: On a sunny day the sand on a beach becomes much hotter than the sea water. The main reason is that:
o: Sand has a much lower specific heat than water
Sand has a much higher specific heat than water
Sand receives far more sunlight than the sea
Water cannot absorb heat from the Sun
x: For the same heat per kilogram, a substance with lower specific heat has a bigger temperature rise. Water's high specific heat keeps it cooler.

q: When an ideal gas is heated at constant volume, the heat supplied goes:
o: Entirely into increasing its internal energy
Entirely into doing work on the surroundings
Partly into internal energy and partly into work
Nowhere, because the temperature cannot change
x: At constant volume ΔV = 0, so the gas does no work. All the heat (nCvΔT) raises its internal energy and so its temperature.

q: A 100 W immersion heater heats 0.5 kg of a liquid for 2 minutes and its temperature rises by 6 K. Ignoring losses, the specific heat of the liquid is:
x: Heat = power × time = 100 × 120 = 12 000 J. c = Q ÷ mΔT = 12 000 ÷ (0.5 × 6) = 4000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Using 2 s instead of 120 s gives about 67.

q: The internal energy of a system is the:
o: Kinetic energy of the system moving as a whole
Sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all its molecules
Heat that the system has given out
Work done on the system by gravity
x: Internal energy is the total of the random kinetic energies and the intermolecular potential energies of the molecules, not the motion of the whole body.

q: A gas takes in 900 J of heat, but its internal energy goes up by only 500 J. The rest leaves as work done by the gas, equal to:
x: Q = ΔU + W, with W the work done by the gas: 900 = 500 + W, so W = 400 J.

q: In an adiabatic process no heat enters or leaves the gas. With W as the work done by the gas, the first law becomes:
x: Putting Q = 0 into Q = ΔU + W gives ΔU = −W: if the gas does work, its internal energy falls by the same amount.

q: In an isothermal change of an ideal gas, which quantity is zero?
o: The work done by the gas
x: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. At constant temperature ΔU = 0, so the heat supplied equals the work done by the gas.

q: A piston does 150 J of work compressing a gas, and meanwhile the gas loses 150 J as heat through the cylinder walls. What happens to its internal energy?
x: Energy gained as work (+150 J) equals energy lost as heat (−150 J), so ΔU = +150 − 150 = 0 and the temperature of an ideal gas stays the same.

q: A gas absorbs 100 J of heat and at the same time 50 J of work is done on it by a piston. The change in its internal energy is:
x: Both the heat supplied and the work done on the gas add energy to it: ΔU = 100 + 50 = +150 J.

q: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1 × 10⁵ Pa from 2 litres to 5 litres while absorbing 800 J of heat. The change in its internal energy is (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³):
x: Work done by the gas = PΔV = 1 × 10⁵ × 3 × 10⁻³ = 300 J. ΔU = Q − W = 800 − 300 = +500 J.

q: According to the first law of thermodynamics, the total energy of an isolated system:
x: An isolated system exchanges no heat or work with its surroundings, so by conservation of energy its total energy stays the same.

q: A heat engine can never give out more work in a cycle than the heat it takes in during that cycle. This follows from:
o: The law of conservation of energy
x: The first law is energy conservation: over a cycle ΔU = 0, so the work output cannot exceed the net heat input.

q: When gas is released quickly from an aerosol can, the can becomes cold. The best explanation is that the escaping gas:
o: Does work in expanding, using some of its internal energy
Absorbs heat from the air and so cools down
Gains internal energy from the can
Loses mass, which lowers its temperature
x: The expansion is too fast for much heat to flow in, so the work done by the gas comes from its internal energy, and its temperature falls.

q: A bullet strikes a wooden block and stops inside it, and both become warm. In terms of energy, this shows that:
o: Energy has been destroyed in the collision
The kinetic energy of the bullet has become internal energy
Heat has been created from nothing
The internal energy of the bullet has become kinetic energy
x: The bullet's kinetic energy is not lost; work done against the wood turns it into internal energy of the bullet and the block, so they warm up.

q: In Joule's experiments on the mechanical equivalent of heat, the amount of work that produced the same heating as 1 calorie was about:
x: Joule found that about 4.2 J of mechanical work gives the same heating as 1 calorie of heat, showing that heat and work are both forms of energy transfer.

q: Using Q = heat supplied to a gas, W = work done by the gas and ΔU = change in internal energy, which set of values is impossible?
x: The first law needs Q = ΔU + W. For 200 J in and 100 J of work out, ΔU must be +100 J, not +300 J; the other sets all satisfy Q = ΔU + W.

q: Water falls 84 m down a waterfall. If all its potential energy became internal energy of the water, its temperature rise would be about (g = 10 m s⁻², specific heat of water 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹):
x: For each kilogram, mgh = mcΔT, so ΔT = gh/c = 10 × 84 ÷ 4200 = 840 ÷ 4200 = 0.2 K. The mass cancels.

q: The numerical value of Cp − Cv for one mole of any ideal gas equals the gas constant, about:
x: For an ideal gas Cp − Cv = R, the molar gas constant, which is about 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

q: A gas behaves ideally and has a molar heat capacity of 33.2 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ when heated at constant pressure. What is its molar heat capacity at constant volume? (R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
x: Cv = Cp − R = 33.2 − 8.3 = 24.9 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Adding R instead of subtracting gives 41.5, and dividing gives 4.0.

q: For an ideal gas of molar mass M, the difference between the specific heats per kilogram, cp − cv, is equal to:
x: Per mole, Cp − Cv = R. Dividing by the molar mass M (kg per mole) changes per-mole values into per-kilogram values, so cp − cv = R/M.

q: In deriving Cp − Cv = R, the first law is applied to n moles heated through ΔT at constant pressure. The heat supplied, nCpΔT, is set equal to:
x: At constant pressure the heat raises the internal energy (nCvΔT) and does work PΔV. With PΔV = nRΔT this gives Cp = Cv + R.

q: The relation Cp − Cv = R shows that the molar gas constant R has the same unit as:
x: R is the difference of two molar specific heats, so it is measured in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the unit of molar specific heat.

q: If an ideal gas has Cv equal to twice the gas constant, what is the value of γ = Cp/Cv?
x: Cp = Cv + R = 3R, so γ = 3R ÷ 2R = 1.5. Giving Cp/Cv as Cv/Cp gives 0.67.

q: For an ideal gas the ratio γ = Cp/Cv is 1.4. Using Cp − Cv = R, its molar specific heat at constant volume Cv is:
x: Cp = 1.4Cv, so 1.4Cv − Cv = R, giving 0.4Cv = R and Cv = R/0.4 = 2.5R. Then Cp = 3.5R, which is the tempting wrong choice.
